name: Trading 212
summary: Limited data. Candidate reports describe a short screen and a one-on-one technical round, with longer loops for senior roles. Job postings describe a Java 17/21 and Spring, Kafka and PostgreSQL stack. Glassdoor and the company careers page could not be opened from here, so the detail below comes from search summaries of those pages.
confidence: Reported = candidate reports seen in search summaries (Glassdoor, not opened directly). Likely = inferred from job postings or generic prep guides. Nothing here is confirmed by the company.

process.format: Phone screen. One Software Engineer report (Sofia office): 6 basic computer science questions in about 15 minutes. The questions were not listed.
One Glassdoor summary puts the split of Software Engineer candidates at about 40% phone interview, 40% one-on-one interview and 20% skills test.
Senior Backend candidate: HR screen, technical screen, then a second HR interview. The technical part was described as structured but shallow for a senior role.

Another Software Engineer report: screening, HR, a three-hour technical round onsite, then an interview with the Head of Engineering. A separate account mentions a behavioural interview and a final interview with a founder.
A third-party listing says the process is a recruiter conversation, a code review, a system design round and a managerial interview. Unverified, and it does not cite a candidate.
A February 2025 Glassdoor review describes an in-person technical interview that ran long. The questions were not especially hard, but the round was tiring.
Reports put the whole process at about 1 to 2 weeks. Glassdoor's overall average is 17.5 days.
A prep guide describes a 30-minute recruiter screen, a 45 to 60 minute technical round (coding or system design) and a 45-minute behavioural round. It says nothing specific about Trading 212.

topics.name: Stack
topics.what: Java 17 or 21 with Spring, Kafka, PostgreSQL, Redis, ClickHouse, Elasticsearch, Docker and Kubernetes, AWS, Grafana. From job postings, which disagree on the Java version. Go, Node.js and TypeScript also appear on some postings.

study_plan.how: Open two current Trading 212 backend postings. Note the Java version (17 or 21), the frameworks and the messaging tool. Build your notes around what they say, not around this page.

Create a PostgreSQL table with a few million rows. Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE, add an index, run it again and explain the difference. Write the double-booking fix as one conditional UPDATE, then test two concurrent requests against it. Learn the four isolation levels and what each one prevents.

Explain how the garbage collector finds unreachable objects, then how a leak still happens. Know the equals and hashCode contract, how HashMap uses them, and why ThreadLocal leaks in a thread pool. On Java 21, know what virtual threads change and what they do not.

Learn the rules that make @Transactional fail silently: self-invocation, non-public methods, and checked exceptions that do not roll back by default. Build a small Kafka consumer, then make it idempotent. Learn the outbox pattern and explain it in two sentences.

Practise the reported video upload problem and one booking or payments problem. Speak your answer out loud for 45 minutes. Start with requirements and numbers, draw the data flow, then cover failures: retries, duplicates, a slow dependency and a region outage.
Run two mocks: one 45-minute coding round and one 45-minute design round. Ask a friend to interrupt with follow-up questions. Record yourself and note where you hesitate.

Prepare three stories: a production incident you fixed, a decision you pushed back on, and a time you owned a problem outside your remit. Read Trading 212's product pages and any public engineering posts, and be ready to say why a trading platform needs correct, reliable code.

questions.q: What is database sharding, and what problem does it solve?
questions.a: Sharding splits one dataset across several database instances by a key, such as user id. It spreads storage and write load when one machine can't handle them. The cost is cross-shard queries, rebalancing and harder transactions.

questions.q: How does a database index speed up a query, and what does it cost?
questions.a: An index is a sorted structure, usually a B-tree, on one or more columns. Lookups go from scanning every row to a few tree steps. It costs extra storage, slower writes, and an index can't help a query that doesn't filter or sort on its columns.

questions.q: How do Java memory leaks happen, even with a garbage collector?
questions.a: The collector frees objects that can't be reached. A leak happens when objects stay reachable by mistake, such as a static map that grows, a listener that is never removed, or a ThreadLocal that is never cleared in a pool.

questions.q: How would you prevent double booking when two services can accept the same request?
questions.a: Make the booking a single atomic step on one owner, such as a unique constraint or a conditional update (for example UPDATE ... WHERE status = 'free'). Use idempotency keys for retries. Don't rely on a read-then-write across services.

questions.q: What is the difference between repeatable read and serializable isolation?
questions.a: Repeatable read keeps the rows a transaction has read stable, but can still allow phantom rows in a range query, depending on the database. Serializable makes concurrent transactions behave as if they ran one at a time, at the cost of more blocking or retries.

questions.q: Design a video upload system like YouTube.
questions.a: Clarify first: maximum file size, resumable uploads, how fast a video must be playable, and scale. The client asks the API for a presigned upload URL and sends the file in chunks straight to object storage, so big files skip the app servers. The API stores metadata (id, owner, status) in PostgreSQL. When the upload completes, a message starts async transcoding into several resolutions. Workers write the renditions back to storage and update the status. Serve through a CDN. Cover retries, duplicate upload-complete events, and what the user sees while processing.

questions.q: How do you stop a Kafka consumer from processing the same message twice?
questions.a: You can't fully. Kafka delivers at least once, so a retry or a consumer rebalance can deliver a message again. Make the handler idempotent: record the message id in the same database transaction as the side effect, under a unique constraint, or use a natural idempotent write such as an upsert. Commit the offset only after the work is saved.

questions.q: Why can a @Transactional method run without a transaction when it is called from the same class?
questions.a: Spring applies @Transactional through a proxy. A call from another method in the same class (this.method()) skips the proxy, so no transaction starts. The same happens for non-public methods, which are not proxied by default. Fix it by moving the method to another bean, or by calling it through the proxy.

questions.q: What does backward compatibility mean for an API or a stored message format?
questions.a: Old clients and old stored data keep working after a change. Add optional fields rather than renaming or removing them, version breaking changes, and deploy readers before writers when the format changes.

questions.q: When would Go be a better fit than Java for a microservice?
questions.a: Go suits small services with fast start-up, low memory use and simple concurrency. Java suits teams with large existing Spring code, rich libraries and strong tooling. Pick by team skills, operations and the services' workload, not by language alone.
